Red seabream (Pagrus major) spawning occurs in coastal waters during spring, with egg fertilization following a broadcast spawning event. The resulting fertilized eggs are small and pelagic, with a diameter of approximately one millimeter. From this egg size, the calculated wet weight at birth is roughly 0.00052 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00052 grams], a value typical for teleost embryos that rely on endogenous yolk reserves. Incubation and embryonic development proceed rapidly in captivity; experimental data indicate that at a stable temperature of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C], the period from fertilization to hatching lasts approximately 9.5 days [ab = approximately 9.5 days]. This relatively brief developmental interval is consistent with the energetic demands of a pelagic larva that must transition quickly to exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larva, or protolarva, emerges with a minimal body mass and relies entirely on its yolk supply until mouth opening and first feeding commence several days later. Laboratory trials show that hatching success is highest when thermal conditions remain close to this optimal level, underscoring the importance of temperature for early life stage survival in this commercially valuable sparid.

A key life-history milestone for Pagrus major is the attainment of sexual maturation, which is closely tied to body size rather than strictly age. Field surveys and aquaculture records consistently show that individuals reach puberty at a total length of approximately 34.3 cm [Lp = approximately 34.3 cm]. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is about 578 grams [Wwp = about 578 grams], representing a substantial increase from the minute larval mass. The reproductive investment at this stage is considerable; once mature, a female can produce a large number of eggs per spawning event. Under optimal thermal conditions of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate has been estimated at approximately 12,452 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 12,452 eggs per day], corresponding to a per-spawning fecundity of about 12,452 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = about 12,452 eggs per spawning event] and a daily spawning frequency [F_R_i = daily spawning frequency] during the peak of the breeding season. This high fecundity is an adaptation to the high mortality rates experienced by pelagic eggs and larvae.

Growth in Red seabream continues well beyond the onset of maturity, with individuals eventually approaching a maximum size. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is approximately 100 cm [Li = approximately 100 cm], a value that represents the upper limit of somatic growth observed in wild populations. At this length, the corresponding ultimate wet weight can exceed 14.8 kilograms [Wwi = 14.8 kilograms], indicating a robust, deep-bodied morphology typical of large sparids. The transition from a 578-gram (578 grams) [Wwp = 578 grams] fish at puberty to a 14.8-kilogram (14.8 kilograms) [Wwi = 14.8 kilograms] adult requires several years of sustained feeding and favorable environmental conditions. Growth rates are highest during the juvenile and sub-adult stages, then decelerate markedly as the fish approach their maximum length. Comparative data from related species in the family Sparidae suggest that this size trajectory is shaped by a trade-off between investment in somatic growth and the high energetic demands of repeated annual spawning events.

Longevity is a critical parameter for understanding population dynamics and the reproductive value of older individuals in the stock. Under the favorable thermal regime of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C], the maximum lifespan of Pagrus major has been estimated at approximately 26 years [am = approximately 26 years]. This extended lifespan classifies the species as a long-lived, iteroparous teleost, allowing multiple reproductive seasons over the course of an individual's life. In comparison, the age at birth is a remarkably short 9.5 days [ab = 9.5 days], highlighting the dramatic contrast between the vulnerable larval stage and the long-lived, fecund adult form at a temperature of 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C]. A female that reaches 34.3 cm [Lp = 34.3 cm] at puberty will therefore have a reproductive window spanning more than two decades if she survives to the maximum recorded age. Natural mortality rates are highest during the egg and larval phases, but once individuals recruit to the benthic juvenile stage, their survival prospects improve considerably, contributing to the species' resilience under moderate fishing pressure.

The physiological ecology of Pagrus major is further illuminated by comparing its body size metrics. The wet weight at birth of roughly 0.00052 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00052 grams] is minuscule relative to the ultimate wet weight of 14.8 kilograms [Wwi = 14.8 kilograms], representing more than a 28-million-fold increase in biomass from the fertilized egg to the largest adults. This extraordinary growth trajectory is supported by a diet that shifts from planktonic prey in the larval stage to benthic crustaceans and mollusks in juveniles and adults. The total length at puberty of 34.3 cm [Lp = 34.3 cm] is reached within the first few years of life, while the ultimate total length of 100 cm [Li = 100 cm] is achieved only after many years of slow, decelerating growth. Thermal conditions throughout life remain important; the key developmental milestones of hatching at 9.5 days [ab = 9.5 days] and the attainment of a lifespan of 26 years [am = 26 years] were both documented at 21.8 °C [T = 21.8 °C], a temperature that appears near-optimal for this temperate species.
